title: A Postcards for the Silence
premise: After her mother's funeral, Tamsin Sterling returns to the family house to catalog its contents for sale, discovering a drawer of unsent postcards written in a language she cannot read. The language is Vessic, spoken fluently by only one living person, an elderly neighbor named Ilse Marchetti, who agrees to teach Tamsin in exchange for help recording her vocabulary before the housing estate that will demolish both their homes. As lessons deepen, Tamsin decodes the postcards—her mother's decades-long correspondence with a woman she loved but never named—and must choose between selling the house as duty demands or preserving the truth it holds. The novel ends on demolition day with Tamsin reading the final postcard aloud at the graveside, having become Vessic's second-to-last speaker and, finally, her mother's daughter.
about_author: Jude Thackeray is the pen name of a former archivist who spent twelve years cataloging private letters in estate sales before turning to fiction. They write about inheritance, silence, and the languages families invent to avoid saying what they mean.

chapters.title: The Inventory Begins
chapters.summary: Tamsin, POV, returns to the empty family house after the funeral and begins the methodical cataloging her mother's will requires. Each object gets a number; each number reminds her of something never said. Emotional beat: grief disguised as competence.

chapters.title: A Drawer That Doesn't Fit
chapters.summary: Still Tamsin's POV. While measuring the study she finds a locked drawer containing forty-one postcards, all addressed to 'M,' all written in an alphabet she doesn't recognize. She pockets one without logging it—the first dishonest act of her careful life.

chapters.title: The Last Speaker
chapters.summary: Tamsin tracks the script to Ilse Marchetti, ninety-one, the final fluent speaker of Vessic, who lives two streets away under a demolition notice. Ilse agrees to translate one card only if Tamsin becomes her student. Beat: reluctant bargain, first spark of purpose.

chapters.title: First Words
chapters.summary: First lesson: Ilse teaches greetings, refuses to translate the card, and records everything on a dying tape recorder. Tamsin struggles with sounds her mouth was never taught. Beat: humiliation giving way to unexpected tenderness between two keepers of dead things.

chapters.title: What the House Remembers
chapters.summary: Tamsin catalogs the bedrooms and unearths her mother's youth—photographs of a woman named Renata, cropped from every frame. Flashbacks shift briefly to the mother's voice through marginalia. Beat: the inventory starts feeling like an interrogation.

chapters.title: Grammar of Avoidance
chapters.summary: Ilse reveals Vessic has no word for 'goodbye,' only constructions meaning 'until' or 'instead.' Tamsin recognizes her own family's dialect of deflection. Beat: the language lesson becomes a mirror; Tamsin leaves early, shaken.

chapters.title: Card Number Seven
chapters.summary: Against Ilse's advice, Tamsin insists on translating card seven. It reads: 'I have told him nothing and I am tired of the shape of my silence.' Beat: first confirmation the postcards were love letters, and that her father may never have known.

chapters.title: The Estate Agent
chapters.summary: Tamsin's brother Marcus arrives to push the sale, armed with offers and a demolition timeline. Their argument exposes old roles: he performs grief, she performs order. Beat: duty tightens; the deadline becomes real—sixty days.

chapters.title: Renata
chapters.summary: Ilse finally names the correspondent: Renata Oduya, her own cousin, who left for Lagos in 1974 and died last spring. The three women formed a triangle of exile, silence, and letters. Beat: Tamsin realizes she inherited not just a house but an unfinished sentence.

chapters.title: Vocabulary of Weather
chapters.summary: Lessons continue; Ilse teaches weather words because, she says, 'you can say anything about the rain.' Tamsin begins writing her own unsent postcards. Beat: quiet joy, the first chapter where learning feels like freedom rather than excavation.

chapters.title: Marcus Finds the Drawer
chapters.summary: Marcus discovers the open drawer and accuses Tamsin of hiding assets—or worse, of manufacturing scandal to delay the sale. He takes a card as leverage. Beat: betrayal inside the family; stakes shift from private to legal.

chapters.title: The Tape Recorder Dies
chapters.summary: Ilse's recorder fails mid-session, erasing a week of vocabulary. Tamsin stays overnight transcribing from memory, and Ilse tells the story of choosing to stop speaking Vessic after her husband called it shameful. Beat: intimacy deepens; the cost of silence made explicit.

chapters.title: An Offer on the House
chapters.summary: A developer's offer arrives—generous, immediate, contingent on vacant possession before demolition. Marcus signs intent papers without telling her. Beat: rising pressure; Tamsin must decide what the house is for.

chapters.title: The Untranslatable Sentence
chapters.summary: Ilse attempts card forty-one, the last one, and stops. Some sentences, she says, can be translated but not survived. She gives Tamsin the grammar to do it alone. Beat: the teacher steps back; the student must cross over by herself.

chapters.title: Renata's Reply
chapters.summary: Researching Renata, Tamsin finds a returned letter marked undeliverable in 1975—the moment her mother's correspondence stopped. Her mother wrote into silence for thirty years anyway. Beat: devastating empathy; anger at her mother dissolves into mourning for her.

chapters.title: Demolition Notice Served
chapters.summary: Official notices go up on both houses. Ilse refuses relocation to a care facility outside the district. Tamsin petitions the council using the language's endangered status, her first public act. Beat: invisibility ends; small courage, long odds.

chapters.title: What Marcus Carried
chapters.summary: Marcus confesses he knew about Renata—he found a card at fifteen and chose his father's peace over his mother's truth. Siblings reconcile imperfectly over the drawer. Beat: catharsis; the family's silence revealed as collective, not solitary.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: At the council hearing, Tamsin speaks partly in Vessic—a language the officials cannot ignore once Ilse stands beside her. They win a stay of two weeks, nothing more. Beat: triumph shadowed by limits; time now counts down in days.

chapters.title: Card Forty-One, Translated
chapters.summary: Alone at night, Tamsin translates the final card: 'If I could say it in your language I would have said: you were the life I chose instead.' She weeps, then copies it out twice. Beat: climax of understanding; the untranslatable survived.

chapters.title: Two Weeks
chapters.summary: Tamsin and Ilse record a complete spoken archive of Vessic—every word Ilse can give—while Marcus files to convert the house into a small language-and-letters archive instead of selling. Beat: urgent, luminous work against the clock.

chapters.title: Demolition Day
chapters.summary: The houses come down. Tamsin reads card forty-one aloud at their mother's grave, then mails a copy to Renata's granddaughter in Lagos. Ilse watches the walls fall and says the Vessic word for 'instead.' Beat: release; grief and love said at last.

chapters.title: Postscript: Second-to-Last Speaker
chapters.summary: Months later, Tamsin receives a letter from Lagos: Renata's granddaughter wants to learn. Lessons begin again, now by postcard, sent and answered. Beat: resolution—the silence broken, the language alive, identity chosen rather than inherited.
